case_study_insert.main_stem: BrightPath Learning (BPL) is a private limited company in the education sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2013 by Samuel Okafor, it delivers short courses and tutoring to school pupils and adult learners, and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. BPL plans to invest $540,000 in a new digital learning studio and e-learning platform, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and a $240,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $200,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $72 for a course unit, and currently delivers 10,000 units a year. BPL faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14%, and complaints about the quality of online course materials are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — October 2025: A survey of 800 parents and adult learners found 67% would pay up to $8 more for live small-group tutoring, and 58% preferred evening classes. Enrolments last quarter were 2,450 units against a target of 2,800. The complaint rate rose to 3.6% of course units, and 31 formal complaints were logged in September. Average course-material download time is 4.1 minutes. 12 of 48 tutors have not completed on-the-job training on the new e-learning platform; an external trainer charges $550 per tutor for a certified course.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of BrightPath Learning for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has cut the base interest rate from 5.5% to 4.75%, reducing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans such as BPL's $300,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $13.20 to $14.15 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for tutoring and support staff. (3) Textbook and digital content licensing costs have risen 8.6% year-on-year, while household spending on private tutoring fell 1.4% over the same period.

questions.question_text: BPL plans to fund part of its $540,000 digital studio with a $300,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for BPL of raising the $240,000 through a share issue instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $240,000 share issue brings in equity that never has to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, so BPL avoids adding further debt service to the $300,000 loan while meeting fixed costs of $200,000 a year. The cash can be spent on the e-learning platform and on resolving the 3.6% complaint rate, rather than being absorbed by finance charges on the $540,000 investment.

Point 2: Equity finance improves the cushion available to absorb losses if enrolments stay at 2,450 units against a 2,800 target, because there is no fixed repayment that could force a cash crisis. It also shares the risk of the new digital studio with investors rather than leaving Samuel Okafor's original business solely exposed to the bank. A larger loan would require repayments even if the e-learning platform takes longer than expected to attract the 10,000 course units needed each year. Investors would also bring skills and contacts that Samuel Okafor can use when negotiating the school partnerships needed to raise enrolments.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to BPL's expansion, enrolments and costs.

questions.question_text: BPL enrolled 2,450 units last quarter against a target of 2,800. Consider local newspaper advertising, referral bonuses for existing learners, or partnerships with local schools. Which should BPL choose to raise enrolments? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper advertising: Print ads could reach parents across the region and raise awareness of the new digital studio. However, response is hard to measure, readership is ageing, and the 58% of surveyed learners who prefer evening classes are not specifically targeted, so much of the spend would be wasted for a 48-employee business already funding a $540,000 expansion.

Referral bonuses for existing learners: Offering a discount to learners who recommend a friend uses the 67% of 800 survey respondents who would pay $8 more for live small-group tutoring as evidence of goodwill. Referrals are cheap and trusted, but growth depends on existing learners acting, and with 14% labour turnover and a 3.6% complaint rate the current customer experience may not encourage recommendations.

Partnerships with local schools: Formal links with schools give BPL direct access to the pupils it already tutors, create a steady flow of evening-course enrolments, and support the 58% preference for evening classes. Agreements take time to negotiate and schools may demand discounted rates, but the channel is repeatable and reaches the 2,800-unit target more reliably than one-off adverts.

School links can also provide tutors with a predictable pipeline, reducing the revenue volatility that makes servicing the $300,000 loan difficult.

Recommendation: BPL should choose partnerships with local schools, backed by small referral bonuses. School links deliver a recurring, targeted pipeline that can close the 350-unit gap (2,800 − 2,450) and fill the new e-learning studio. Newspaper advertising is rejected as unmeasurable and poorly targeted; referral bonuses alone are rejected as too dependent on current satisfaction while the complaint rate is 3.6%.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the options with minimal reference to BPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BPL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why newspaper advertising and referral bonuses alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: BPL uses a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. Explain two benefits for BPL of this approach in tackling the 3.6% complaint rate about online course materials.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Samuel Okafor set clear, uniform standards for course-material quality and require immediate corrections, which is valuable when 31 formal complaints were logged in September and the complaint rate has reached 3.6%. A single decision-maker can act faster than a committee, protecting the 67% of survey respondents willing to pay $8 more for a better service.

Point 2: A hierarchical structure gives a clear chain of command and defined responsibility for checking materials before publication, so errors in the e-learning platform can be traced to a named manager. This structure also supports the 48 staff through 14% labour turnover by making roles and reporting lines explicit, reducing confusion when new tutors join and helping BPL reach its 2,800-unit enrolment target through consistent delivery. Clear responsibilities are particularly valuable with 14% labour turnover, because new tutors can see who checks their work and who approves corrections to the e-learning materials, reducing the chance of repeated errors reaching learners.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to BPL's complaints, turnover and e-learning platform.

questions.question_text: BPL must train 12 of 48 tutors on the new e-learning platform. Consider on-the-job training or an external certified course at $550 per tutor. Which should BPL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching tutors while they prepare and deliver live small-group sessions is directly relevant to BPL's own e-learning platform, costs no fees, and keeps all 12 tutors teaching the 10,000 course units, which matters while enrolments are only 2,450 against a 2,800 target. It also allows immediate correction of the 3.6% complaint rate. The drawback is that senior tutors lose time from their own teaching, standards can vary between coaches, and there is no external certificate to reassure parents.

External certified course: At $550 per tutor, training all 12 costs $6,600 (12 × $550), a small fraction of the $540,000 studio investment. It gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate that supports quality assurance claims, and it removes tutors from the platform so learning is not squeezed by urgent marking. However, it takes 12 of 48 tutors away from delivery temporarily, and generic course content may not match BPL's platform settings without follow-up coaching.

There is also a retention angle: with labour turnover at 14%, a certificate can make the 12 tutors more willing to stay, whereas on-the-job training leaves them with no portable qualification. BPL should weigh that against the immediate need to keep 2,450 enrolments rising toward 2,800.

Decision: BPL should choose on-the-job training first, adding short certified sessions for the most senior tutors later. On-the-job training protects teaching capacity when enrolments are short of target, is free, and is platform-specific; full external training is rejected because losing 12 tutors would deepen the 3.6% complaint problem and the $6,600 fee duplicates skills that can be learned while working.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to BPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of BPL's enrolments and costs.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to the e-learning platform.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BPL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $200,000 ÷ ($72 − $22) = $200,000 ÷ $50 = 4,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 4,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $72 − $22 = $50. Answer: contribution per unit is $50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BPL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 4,000-unit break-even output with 10,000 units delivered shows a margin of safety of 6,000 units, giving room to pursue the 2,800-unit quarterly enrolment target without immediate loss.
2. Contribution of $50 a unit lets managers model the $8 premium for live small-group tutoring; adding it would raise contribution to $58 on those places, showing how quickly the 3.6% complaint problem could be addressed.
3. With fixed costs of $200,000 and contribution of $50, managers can set the volume needed to service the $300,000 loan before the $540,000 studio commitment is extended further.
4. Average total cost ($200,000 ÷ 10,000 + $22 = $42) can be tracked each quarter to check that the 8.6% licensing-cost inflation is not eroding margins and that the 4.1-minute download time is not adding waste.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 4,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 10,000-unit output; $8 premium modelling; loan-service volume for the $300,000 loan; and average total cost of $42 to monitor licensing inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BPL's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has BPL's performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 16.0%

Detailed workings: 2024: 720 ÷ 1,800 × 100 = 40.0%; 216 ÷ 1,800 × 100 = 12.0%; 216 ÷ 1,800 × 100 = 12.0%. 2025: 972 ÷ 2,160 × 100 = 45.0%; 324 ÷ 2,160 × 100 = 15.0%; 324 ÷ 2,025 × 100 = 16.0%. Revenue grew to $2,160,000 while cost of sales rose only to $1,188,000, so the first margin widened; operating profit reached $324,000 as the second margin strengthened. Capital employed increased to $2,025,000, yet the return on that larger base still improved. Interest payable fell from $45,000 to $40,000, leaving more operating profit for reinvestment.

Evaluation: All three measures moved in the right direction. The rise from 40.0% to 45.0% shows BPL is controlling the direct costs of course delivery even as licensing costs inflate by 8.6%. The move from 12.0% to 15.0% indicates fixed costs of $200,000 are being spread over more of the 10,000 course units, and the fall in interest payable helps. The return on capital employed rising from 12.0% to 16.0% is the strongest evidence because it shows the larger $2,025,000 asset base is being used more effectively, which supports the $540,000 studio investment. A limitation is that no receivables or cash data are shown, so a better income statement does not prove BPL can meet short-term obligations; the $300,000 loan still requires repayment.

Conclusion: BPL's performance has improved. Every measure rose, and the 16.0% return on capital employed confirms that expansion is adding value rather than simply increasing revenue.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate percentage calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates all three measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BPL of charging the $8 premium for live small-group tutoring identified in its market research.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 800 parents and learners found that 67% would pay up to $8 more for live small-group tutoring, so the premium could lift the $72 selling price toward $80 on those places and raise contribution per unit from $50 to $58. That extra contribution would help cover fixed costs of $200,000 a year, fund the $540,000 e-learning studio and give BPL resources to cut the 3.6% complaint rate on course materials.

Disadvantage: the remaining respondents who would not pay more may reject the higher price, and with enrolments already at 2,450 against a 2,800 target a price rise could reduce demand further and leave tutor capacity idle. The 58% who prefer evening classes may also expect that convenience at the existing price, so a premium on small-group sessions could deepen complaints unless the quality of materials improves at the same time. BPL could test the surcharge on the evening classes favoured by 58% of respondents before extending it to all courses.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to BPL's survey, contribution and enrolment data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate cut to 4.75%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 8.6% rise in content licensing costs will affect BPL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate cut (5.5% to 4.75%): If BPL's $300,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost falls by 0.75% of $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). That is a useful saving against fixed costs of $200,000, and cheaper credit also makes future borrowing for the $540,000 studio less expensive. If the loan is fixed-rate the immediate effect is zero, so this is the smallest and least certain of the three changes.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $14.15 an hour): With a workforce of 48, including tutoring and support roles, this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage total can be invented. The defensible comparison is productivity: 10,000 units ÷ 48 staff = 208.3 units per worker, so the rise is sustainable only if output per tutor holds or grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $50 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Content licensing inflation (8.6%): The $22 variable cost is not broken down in the insert, so only a bound is possible: if the whole variable cost rose 8.6% it would add 0.086 × $22 = $1.89 per unit; at 10,000 units that is $18,900 a year. This hits every course unit directly, and with household tutoring spending down 1.4% BPL has limited ability to pass it on, though the $8 small-group premium offers partial recovery.

Conclusion: The 8.6% rise in licensing costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 10,000 units and erodes the $50 contribution that funds the $540,000 expansion, and falling demand limits pricing power; the interest cut saves only $2,250 and the wage effect, while real, cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity and the premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to BPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on BPL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that licensing inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
